html:
Cayenne was the French colony on the Guiana coast of South America, named after its chief town on an island at the mouth of the Cayenne River. On maps of the 1600s and 1700s the colony often goes by the town's name; later it was called French Guiana, and Cayenne is still its capital.

French settlers tried and failed here several times before a lasting colony took hold in 1664. In the wars of the 1600s the Dutch and English each held it briefly, and Portuguese troops from Brazil occupied it from 1809 to 1817.

The colony stayed small. Planters grew sugar, annatto dye, cotton and later coffee, worked by Africans brought through the Atlantic slave trade. Disease, heat and isolation kept free settlers away, unlike the richer sugar island of Saint-Domingue. Its neighbour to the west was Dutch Suriname.

France later used the colony as a prison, most famously at Devil's Island. In 1946 it became an overseas department of France.
